aAbout: GodsView AI is a hosted live world map: a 2D map (MapLibre GL and deck.gl) with a Cesium 3D globe, fed by OpenSky aircraft, aisstream.io ships, satellites, earthquakes, NASA fire data, weather and news. Its signature piece is the Ops Center, which merges duplicate reports of the same event from agencies like USGS, GDACS and GDELT and scores every incident from 0 to 100, with country risk ratings. A free account opens the map; Pro unlocks the full camera catalogue, the photoreal globe, alerts and flight replay.
aStrengths: GodsView AI is the operational tool: the Ops Center turns a firehose of agency reports into a scored, deduplicated incident register with country risk — something Liveuamap's editorial map doesn't attempt. Add a claimed ~229,000-camera catalogue, live flights and ships, Pro alerts (emergency squawks, quakes, watch areas), flight replay, a news video wall, briefs you can export, and a lifetime pricing option, and it's the better pick for anyone who wants the whole moving world — not just its conflicts — monitored from any browser.
bAbout: Liveuamap — the Live Universal Awareness Map — is an independent global news and information site founded in 2014 to cover the Ukrainian conflict, and expanded by viewer request to more than 30 regions and topics today. It plots conflicts, human rights issues, protests, terrorism, weapons deployment, health matters, natural disasters and weather stories on per-region maps, keeping a complete chronological archive of past events. Its method is editorial: proprietary AI web crawlers surface candidate stories, which a group of expert analysts fact-checks before editors decide what appears on the map. It runs from EU-based infrastructure under Liveuamap LLC (Virginia, USA), is free on the web and in its iOS and Android apps, and carries advertising.
bStrengths: Liveuamap is the established editorial record: twelve years of analyst fact-checked conflict reporting across 30+ regions, organised map-first with a chronological archive researchers can actually cite — the kind of trust a scored incident feed can't shortcut. It's free to read with no account, it has proper native iOS and Android apps where GodsView has only the browser, and its paid tiers are the cheapest in this comparison — ad-free viewing for $9.54 a half-year, PRO from $7/month. For following a specific conflict region closely, it's the specialist.
betterAnswer: They solve different problems. GodsView AI is a hosted live map for monitoring everything at once — cameras, flights, ships, satellites and a scored incident register — free with an account, paid to unlock. Liveuamap is an editorial news map: no cameras, no flights, no ships, no globe, but analyst fact-checked conflict reporting across 30+ regions with an archive going back years, free to read. If you want breadth and live assets, open GodsView AI; if you want one conflict followed properly, open Liveuamap.

faqs.a: No — they are unrelated products from different operators. GodsView AI is a hosted live map by founder Jijo John, built around cameras, traffic layers and a scored Ops Center. Liveuamap is an independent news site run by Liveuamap LLC, founded in 2014, built around analyst fact-checked regional reporting. GodsView AI is also a different product from the open-source God's Eye View, a distinction GodsView states on its own site.
faqs.q: Is GodsView AI the same as Liveuamap?

faqs.a: Both are free to use, differently. Liveuamap's web maps are publicly accessible with no account described as required, supported by advertising — though joint regions and previous years' historic data are no longer in the free version. GodsView AI requires a free account, and its free tier carries ads, a 30-minute viewing pause, one AI question a day and a maximum of 2 open cameras.

Only GodsView AI. It claims a catalogue of about 229,000 public cameras in about 174 countries, with 2 open on the free tier and the full catalogue on Pro. Liveuamap has no camera network — it plots reported events, not streams. For comparison, WorldEye's directory lists 74,229 public cameras, open on its free map.
faqs.q: Which has live cameras, GodsView AI or Liveuamap?

faqs.a: Liveuamap. It has covered conflicts since 2014 across more than 30 regions, with stories surfaced by AI crawlers and fact-checked by expert analysts before editors publish them, plus a complete chronological archive. GodsView AI covers conflict zones as incident feeds scored by its Ops Center — broader and faster-moving, but not an analyst-edited regional desk.
faqs.q: Which is better for following a conflict like Ukraine?

faqs.a: GodsView AI, on both counts. It tracks live aircraft from OpenSky and live vessels from aisstream.io as core layers. Liveuamap documents no flight or ship tracking — its map carries reported events only.
faqs.q: Which tracks live flights and ships?

faqs.a: Liveuamap charges less at the bottom end — an ad-free account is $9.54 per half-year, and PRO starts from $7/month, adding satellite maps, custom regions, all regions and events, earlier history and data export. GodsView Pro is $10.99/month, $99.99/year or $199.99 lifetime. No free trial is stated for either on their official pages.

intro: GodsView AI and Liveuamap are both live maps of a troubled world, built a decade apart for different ideas of what 'live' means. Liveuamap, founded in 2014 during the Ukraine conflict, is an editorial product: analyst fact-checked events across more than 30 regions, mapped and archived, free to read. GodsView AI is a hosted sensor map: flights, ships, satellites, earthquakes, fires and a claimed ~229,000 cameras, with an Ops Center that scores every incident 0–100. One reports the world; the other instruments it. And the standing disambiguation: GodsView AI is a hosted product by founder Jijo John and, by its own statement, has no affiliation with the open-source God's Eye View project.
pricingA: GodsView AI is free with a free account — with banner ads, a 30-minute live-viewing pause (reload to continue), one AI question a day and two open cameras. Pro costs $10.99/month, $99.99/year or $199.99 as a one-time lifetime plan (no free trial), and unlocks the full ~229,000-camera catalogue, the photoreal 3D globe, military aircraft, NOTAMs, alerts and flight replay.
pricingB: Liveuamap is free on the web with advertising; the free version no longer shows joint regions or historic data for previous years. An ad-free account costs $9.54 per half-year and, in its own words, 'removes advertising only' — it does not enable satellite maps. PRO starts from $7/month and removes advertising, enables satellite maps from Google and Mapbox, allows custom regions, and opens additional features including location search, earlier history, all regions and events, notifications and data export. Enterprise and API services are offered without published prices, and no free trial is stated on its official pages.

verdictA: Choose GodsView AI if you want the whole instrumented world in one browser tab — scored incidents, live traffic, cameras and alerts — and you're happy creating a free account to open it.
verdictB: Choose Liveuamap if you follow specific conflicts closely and want analyst fact-checked regional reporting with a deep archive — free to read, with the cheapest paid tiers here.
verdictLine: Liveuamap reports the world: twelve years of fact-checked events, region by region. GodsView AI instruments it: cameras, traffic and scored incidents on one map. Depth of reporting points one way; breadth of live data points the other.
worldEye: WorldEye differs from both in the same way: it's a hosted 3D globe that opens free in any browser with no signup at all — no GodsView-style account wall — and it's built around watching places live, which Liveuamap doesn't do. Its directory lists 74,229 public cameras across 105 countries, alongside live flights, ships, satellites, weather, earthquakes and wildfires. It neither scores incidents like GodsView's Ops Center nor matches Liveuamap's analyst-edited archive, and its Pro tier ($7.99/week, $13.99/month or $74.99/year) adds an OSINT toolkit and intel feeds for people who work the map actively.
